fuentes/instrucciones-a-los-mayordomos-d.texto: Regulations that Rosas wrote for the stewards and foremen of his estancias, with detailed rules on the care of livestock, branding, sowing, the treatment and discipline of the peones, and accounts. They show how a large cattle estancia of Buenos Aires province operated and the command style of their author before he entered politics.
It is one of the few extensive texts written by Rosas and a source on the economy and rural labor of the pampas in the first decades of independence.

fuentes/carta-de-la-hacienda-de-figueroa.texto: Letter from the Hacienda de Figueroa
Hacienda de Figueroa (San Antonio de Areco)

Letter of December 20, 1834 that Rosas wrote to Facundo Quiroga, who was heading north to mediate between the governments of Salta and Tucumán. It holds that it was not the moment to decree a constitution: first each province had to organize itself and pacify, and only then could a congress meet; a constitution imposed beforehand would produce more war and anarchy. Quiroga was murdered at Barranca Yaco on his return from that mission, in February 1835.

It is the text in which Rosas set out his argument for postponing constitutional organization, which his opponents cited as proof that he never wanted a constitution and his defenders cited as a sign of political prudence.

fuentes/ley-de-la-suma-del-poder-publico.texto: Law of March 7, 1835 (grant of public power)
Chamber of Representatives of the Province of Buenos Aires

Law of the Chamber of Representatives that named Rosas governor for five years and vested in him “the full sum of public power” of the province, with no restrictions other than preserving and defending the Catholic religion and upholding the federal cause. The exercise of that power would last as long as the governor considered necessary. Rosas asked that the election be ratified by a plebiscite of the city's inhabitants, which was held from March 26 to 28, 1835.

It is the legal basis of Rosas's second government: it concentrated executive, legislative and judicial power in his hands for seventeen years, and it was the main charge in the trial the Buenos Aires legislature opened against him in 1857.

fuentes/ley-de-aduana-1835/resumen.texto: Law signed by Rosas and his Minister of Finance, José María Roxas y Patrón, on December 18, 1835, under extraordinary powers, to take effect in 1836. It set a general duty of 17% on imports, 35% on ready-made clothing, footwear, furniture, wines and liquors, and 50% on beer, pastes and saddles; it prohibited the import of hardware, tallow candles and other products manufactured in the country, and the import of foreign wheat and flour while wheat exceeded 50 pesos per fanega. It exempted from duties the seaborne entry of raw hides, wool, tallow, tasajo and other raw livestock products, and the export of grains, flours, salted meats on national ships and domestic manufactures; by land, from the provinces, only yerba and tobacco from Paraguay, Corrientes and Misiones (10%) and cigars (20%) paid duties.

fuentes/ley-de-aduana-1835/por_que_impor.texto: It partly answered the complaints of the interior and Litoral provinces against Porteño free trade, but it left the revenue of the only overseas customs house in Buenos Aires's hands; historians debate how much it really protected provincial crafts.

fuentes/ley-de-aduana-1835/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the law on Wikisource

fuentes/decreto-de-confiscacion-1840/tit.texto: Decree of September 16, 1840 on the Property of the Unitarians

fuentes/decreto-de-confiscacion-1840/res.texto: Decree signed by Rosas and his minister Agustín Garrigós that declared the movable and immovable property of the “savage Unitarian traitors” of the city and countryside “especially liable,” to make good the damage caused to the Federalists by Lavalle's invasion, to cover the treasury's extraordinary expenses and to pay rewards to the defenders of the government. It forbade owners to sell, mortgage or conceal that property, declared void any deeds that did so, and held notaries, brokers, judges and justices of the peace who allowed it liable.

fuentes/decreto-de-confiscacion-1840/por.texto: It was the legal basis for the mass seizure of opponents' property, which passed under state management or was handed to government supporters, and one of the economic pressure tools of Rosismo.

fuentes/decreto-de-confiscacion-1840/lee.texto: Text of the decree on Wikisource

fuentes/la-gaceta-mercantil/autor.texto: Printing house of La Gaceta Mercantil (editors: Pedro de Angelis, Nicolás Mariño and others)

fuentes/la-gaceta-mercantil/resumen.texto: Buenos Aires commercial newspaper founded in 1823 that became Rosas's main organ during his governments. It published decrees, the governor's messages and military reports, including reports of executions of prisoners, under the heading “Long live the Argentine Confederation! Death to the savage Unitarians!”, and it attacked opponents.

fuentes/la-gaceta-mercantil/por_que_impo.texto: It is the main source for the official acts of the period; reports published in its pages were used as evidence in the 1857–1861 trial against Rosas.

fuentes/la-gaceta-mercantil/leer.0.titul.texto: Issue of April 26, 1842, digitized by the Mariano Moreno National Library, on Internet Archive

fuentes/archivo-americano/titulo.texto: American Archive and Spirit of the World Press

fuentes/archivo-americano/resumen.texto: Publication directed by Pedro de Angelis, printed in columns in Spanish, English and French, which reproduced official documents, diplomatic notes and articles from the foreign press to defend Rosas's policy before European and American audiences, especially during the Anglo-French intervention.

fuentes/archivo-americano/por_que_import.texto: It shows how Rosas's government presented its cause abroad and gathers many diplomatic documents from the conflict with France and Great Britain.

fuentes/coleccion-de-angelis/titulo.texto: Collection of Works and Documents Relating to the Ancient and Modern History of the Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/coleccion-de-angelis/resumen.texto: Collection in six volumes, published in Buenos Aires by the Imprenta del Estado, which gathered for the first time chronicles, exploration diaries, descriptions and colonial documents on the Río de la Plata, Patagonia, the Chaco and Paraguay, with preliminary discourses by De Angelis.

fuentes/coleccion-de-angelis/por_que_imp.texto: It was the first major edition of sources on the history of the Río de la Plata and remained a reference for 19th-century historians; it was published under the sponsorship of Rosas's government.

fuentes/proclama-de-rosas-1835/titulo.texto: Proclamation of Rosas on Assuming His Second Government

fuentes/proclama-de-rosas-1835/resumen.texto: Proclamation addressed to the inhabitants of the city and countryside on taking office with the full sum of public power, on April 13, 1835. It attributes the country's ills to a “faction” of corrupt and impious men and calls for pursuing them without rest, so that their punishment would serve as a warning to those who came later.

fuentes/proclama-de-rosas-1835/por_que_i.texto: In Rosas's own words, it announced the persecution of opponents that marked his second government, and his critics cited it as a program of terror.

fuentes/convencion-mackau/autor.texto: Felipe Arana and Baron de Mackau

fuentes/convencion-mackau/resumen.texto: Convention signed on October 29, 1840 aboard the French brig Boulonnaise by Felipe Arana, Rosas's minister, and Baron de Mackau. Buenos Aires recognized compensation to the Frenchmen harmed, to be fixed by arbitrators, and assured them most-favored-nation treatment; France lifted the blockade and returned the island of Martín García and the captured ships. An amnesty was offered to the émigrés who laid down their arms, except the generals and chiefs, and Buenos Aires undertook to respect the independence of Uruguay.

fuentes/convencion-mackau/por_que_import.texto: It ended the French blockade and left Lavalle, the Corrientes leaders and Rivera without French support, which allowed Rosas to turn his forces against the Northern Coalition.

fuentes/convencion-mackau/leer.0.titulo.texto: Text of the convention on Wikisource

fuentes/tratado-arana-southern/resumen.texto: Convention signed in Buenos Aires on November 24, 1849 by Felipe Arana and the British minister Henry Southern. Great Britain undertook to evacuate the island of Martín García, return the Argentine warships and salute the flag of the Confederation with 21 guns, and it acknowledged that navigation of the Paraná was “an internal navigation of the Argentine Confederation, subject only to its laws and regulations,” and that navigation of the Uruguay was shared with the Oriental State.

fuentes/tratado-arana-southern/por_que_i.texto: It closed the British intervention by recognizing Rosas's thesis on the rivers; revisionist historians present it as a diplomatic triumph, and the question of free navigation was reopened after Caseros.

fuentes/tratado-arana-southern/leer.0.ti.texto: Text of the convention on Wikisource

fuentes/convencion-arana-lepredour/autor.texto: Felipe Arana and Admiral Fortunato Lepredour

fuentes/convencion-arana-lepredour/resum.texto: Peace convention signed on August 31, 1850 by Felipe Arana and the French admiral Lepredour, in terms similar to the convention with Great Britain: return of Martín García and the ships, recognition of Argentine sovereignty over the Paraná, and a salute to the flag. The French Assembly delayed its ratification and never approved it.

fuentes/convencion-arana-lepredour/por_q.texto: It effectively ended the French intervention in the Río de la Plata.

fuentes/pronunciamiento-de-urquiza/resum.texto: Decree of the governor of Entre Ríos of May 1, 1851, headed by “Death to the enemies of the National Organization!” Invoking Rosas's age and condition and his repeated resignations, it declared that Entre Ríos resumed the powers of foreign relations and of peace and war that it had delegated to the governor of Buenos Aires under the Federal Pact of 1831, and that the province was now in a position to deal directly with the other governments until the national assembly constituted the Republic.

fuentes/pronunciamiento-de-urquiza/por_q.texto: It opened the break between the Litoral and Rosas that ended at Caseros and in the constitutional organization of 1853.

fuentes/pronunciamiento-de-urquiza/leer..texto: Text of the decree on Wikisource

fuentes/tratado-de-alianza-1851/titulo.texto: Treaty of Alliance between Entre Ríos, Brazil and Uruguay

fuentes/tratado-de-alianza-1851/autor.texto: Governments of Entre Ríos, of the Empire of Brazil and of Montevideo

fuentes/tratado-de-alianza-1851/resumen.texto: Treaty signed in Montevideo on May 29, 1851 by the government of Entre Ríos, the Empire of Brazil and the government of the Defense of Montevideo, to expel Oribe from Uruguayan territory and secure free elections there, with a commitment to turn the alliance against Rosas if he declared war. On November 21, 1851 a new treaty, which Corrientes joined, expressly directed it against Rosas's government, with a loan and Brazilian troops for Urquiza's army.

fuentes/tratado-de-alianza-1851/por_que_.texto: It is the document that united the Argentine Litoral with Brazil and Uruguay against Rosas; revisionists judged it an alliance with foreigners, and its defenders saw it as the necessary path to national organization.

fuentes/juicio-a-los-mazorqueros-1853/au.texto: Courts of the State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/juicio-a-los-mazorqueros-1853/re.texto: Proceedings opened under a decree of the government of Buenos Aires of August 11, 1853, which minister Lorenzo Torres sent to the criminal judge, against former policemen and members of the Mazorca: Silverio Badía, Manuel Troncoso, Antonino Reyes, Fermín Suárez, Estanislao Porto, Manuel Gervasio López, Leandro Alén, Ciriaco Cuitiño, Torcuato Canales and others. The defense argued that they had carried out orders from Rosas, whom no one could disobey, and the courts sentenced several of them to death; the testimony gathered was later used in the case against Rosas.

fuentes/juicio-a-los-mazorqueros-1853/po.texto: They were the first trials for the crimes of the Mazorca, and in them the courts did not accept obedience to Rosas's orders as a valid defense.

fuentes/ley-de-juicio-a-rosas-1857/titul.texto: Law of July 29, 1857 Declaring Rosas Guilty of Treason against the Homeland

fuentes/ley-de-juicio-a-rosas-1857/autor.texto: General Legislative Assembly of the State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/ley-de-juicio-a-rosas-1857/resum.texto: Law of the Senate and the Chamber of Representatives of the State of Buenos Aires that declared Juan Manuel de Rosas “guilty of treason against the homeland for the bloody tyranny he exercised over the people” during his dictatorship, and for having in many cases betrayed his country's independence. It submitted him to the ordinary courts to be tried for the common crimes committed during his government.

fuentes/ley-de-juicio-a-rosas-1857/por_q.texto: It was the basis of the in-absentia trial that ended with Rosas's death sentence in 1861, and it expressed in law the condemnation of Rosismo by liberal Buenos Aires.

fuentes/ley-de-juicio-a-rosas-1857/leer..texto: Text of the law in the 1864 edition of the criminal case against Rosas, on Internet Archive

fuentes/causa-criminal-contra-rosas/titu.texto: Criminal Case against Former Governor Juan Manuel de Rosas before the Ordinary Courts of Buenos Aires

fuentes/causa-criminal-contra-rosas/auto.texto: Courts of the State of Buenos Aires

fuentes/causa-criminal-contra-rosas/resu.texto: 1864 edition of the proceedings against Rosas: the law of July 29, 1857; the indictment by prosecutor Emilio A. Agrelo (1859); witness statements on executions such as those at San Nicolás de los Arroyos (1831) and that of Domingo Cullen (1839); lists of the executed presented as evidence, many with the motive noted (desertion, theft, homicide); and the sentences. The first-instance ruling, issued by judge Sixto Villegas on April 17, 1861, sentenced Rosas “to the ordinary penalty of death, with the aggravating circumstance of treachery,” to return what he had stolen and to be executed at San Benito de Palermo, and it was confirmed by the Superior Tribunal.

fuentes/causa-criminal-contra-rosas/por_.texto: It gathers in a single volume documents and testimony on Rosas's repression, assembled by the prosecution and therefore partisan in slant, which historians use to check against other sources.

fuentes/rosas-y-sus-opositores/resumen.texto: Book published in Montevideo in 1843 gathering Rivera Indarte's writings against Rosas's government: the Revolution of the South, Lavalle's invasion, the peace with France, the “slaughters of October 1840” and the “slaughters of April 1842,” the livestock, trade and the Blood Tables. The 1853 edition added as an appendix the article “Killing Rosas Is a Holy Deed.”

fuentes/rosas-y-sus-opositores/por_que_i.texto: It is the main work denouncing the terror written during Rosas's government; it mixes testimony and documents with propaganda and exaggeration, so historians use it while checking it against other sources.

fuentes/rosas-y-sus-opositores/leer.0.ti.texto: Montevideo edition of 1843 on Internet Archive

fuentes/rosas-y-sus-opositores/leer.1.ti.texto: 1853 edition, with appendices, on Internet Archive

fuentes/tablas-de-sangre/titulo.texto: Blood Tables of the Administrations of Rosas

fuentes/tablas-de-sangre/resumen.texto: Alphabetical list of victims attributed to Rosas's governments and their allies, including Oribe in Uruguay and the Federalist leaders of the interior, published in Rosas and His Opponents. Its final summary, in the 1853 edition, counts 4 poisoned, 3,765 throats cut, 1,393 shot, 722 murdered, 14,920 dead in armed actions and another 1,600 estimated for skirmishes, pursuits and the punishment of deserters, and gives a total of 22,030, although those items add up to 22,404. Two thirds of the total are combat deaths, including soldiers from both sides, and the author presents the figures as a minimum calculation, although many are estimates without names.

fuentes/tablas-de-sangre/por_que_importa.texto: It was the most widely circulated propaganda piece against Rosas in Europe and America; in 1845 the London paper The Atlas, reprinted by the Paris La Presse, claimed that the Lafone house of Montevideo had commissioned and paid for it, and revisionists dismissed it as a pamphlet. Later historians separate the crimes it records from combat deaths: John Lynch estimated about 2,000 victims of the repression between 1829 and 1852, and Gabriel Di Meglio counted about twenty victims of the Mazorca in the city in each of the waves of 1840 and 1842.

fuentes/tablas-de-sangre/leer.0.titulo.texto: Inside Rosas and His Opponents, 1853 edition, on Internet Archive

fuentes/es-accion-santa-matar-a-rosas/ti.texto: Killing Rosas Is a Holy Deed

fuentes/es-accion-santa-matar-a-rosas/re.texto: Article in which Rivera Indarte argues that killing Rosas would be a lawful and meritorious act, drawing on the tradition of tyrannicide: “We would count ourselves very fortunate if this writing moved the heart of some strong man who, plunging a liberating dagger into Rosas's chest, restored to the Río de la Plata its lost happiness.” It circulated in the Montevideo press and was included as an appendix in the 1853 edition of Rosas and His Opponents.

fuentes/es-accion-santa-matar-a-rosas/po.texto: It shows how far the violence of exile press rhetoric went, and defenders of Rosas cited it as proof that his opponents also promoted political murder.

fuentes/es-accion-santa-matar-a-rosas/le.texto: Appendix to Rosas and His Opponents, 1853 edition, on Internet Archive

fuentes/juicio-sobre-el-gobierno-de-rosa.texto: Judgment on the Government of Rosas
Article in El Comercio del Plata

Article by Florencio Varela in El Comercio del Plata describing Rosas's system as founded “on terror and deceit”: a government that proclaimed republican principles and respect for the law while needing acts of violence to sustain itself.
It sums up the liberal exile critique of Rosismo in the pen of its most influential journalist.

fuentes/el-comercio-del-plata/resumen.texto: Newspaper founded by Florencio Varela in Montevideo in 1845, during the Great Siege, which was the main organ of Rosas's opponents. It defended free navigation of the rivers, the Anglo-French intervention and constitutional organization; after Varela's murder in 1848 it continued to be published under the direction of Valentín Alsina.

fuentes/el-comercio-del-plata/por_que_im.texto: It is the main source for the ideas and information of the anti-Rosas emigration between 1845 and 1852.

fuentes/el-iniciador/resumen.texto: Biweekly periodical founded in Montevideo on April 15, 1838 by Andrés Lamas with the help of Miguel Cané, which spread Romanticism and the ideas of the Generation of '37. Young Argentines wrote for it, some still from Buenos Aires, such as Alberdi, Juan María Gutiérrez and Echeverría, and its pages published the credo of the Asociación de Mayo in 1839. It stopped appearing in early 1839.

fuentes/el-iniciador/por_que_importa.texto: It was the first organ of the new Río de la Plata generation and the bridge between the persecuted Porteño youth and the Uruguayan one.

fuentes/la-moda-1837/resumen.texto: Porteño weekly of “music, poetry, literature and customs” published between November 1837 and April 1838, in which Alberdi wrote articles on manners under the pseudonym Figarillo. Under the appearance of a fashion magazine it spread the ideas of the youth of the Salón Literario, and it ceased publication amid the government's distrust.

fuentes/la-moda-1837/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the moment when the Generation of '37 still tried to act in Buenos Aires before going into exile.

fuentes/dogma-socialista/titulo.texto: Socialist Dogma of the Asociación de Mayo

fuentes/dogma-socialista/resumen.texto: Creed of the Association of the Young Argentine Generation, which Echeverría drafted in 1838 as a series of “symbolic words” (association, progress, fraternity, equality, liberty, God, honor, May, democracy and others) and which was published in El Iniciador of Montevideo in 1839. In 1846 he reissued it under the title Socialist Dogma, preceded by a “Retrospective Glance” at the history of the association. It proposes overcoming the division between Unitarians and Federalists, completing the May Revolution with an emancipation of ideas, and founding democracy on the education of the people; “socialist” refers to society, not to the later socialism.

fuentes/dogma-socialista/por_que_importa.texto: It is the political program of the Generation of '37 and one of the antecedents of the ideas of national organization after Caseros.

fuentes/dogma-socialista/leer.0.titulo.texto: Montevideo edition of 1846 on Internet Archive

fuentes/el-matadero/resumen.texto: Story set in the slaughterhouse of southern Buenos Aires during a Lent of the Rosas era: the scarcity of meat, the slaughter of a bull, the death of a child whose throat was accidentally cut and, at the end, the capture and humiliation of a young Unitarian by the Federalists of the slaughterhouse, who dies of rage before being whipped. Echeverría did not publish it; Juan María Gutiérrez made it known in 1871.

fuentes/el-matadero/por_que_importa.texto: It is often considered the first short story in Argentine literature. It presents Rosismo as barbarism, and some later criticism also reads it as testimony to the contempt of the lettered elite for the Federalist plebs.

fuentes/la-cautiva/soporte.texto: Poem included in the book Rimas

fuentes/la-cautiva/resumen.texto: Narrative poem published in 1837 in the book Rimas. María, a white woman held captive by Indigenous people, frees her husband Brian after a malón; they flee across the pampas, he dies in the desert and she dies on learning that their son had had his throat cut.

fuentes/la-cautiva/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first major Argentine Romantic poem and makes the pampas, “the desert,” a literary theme; it presents Indigenous people as savages, an image that later criticism linked to the expansion of the frontier.

fuentes/fragmento-preliminar/titulo.texto: Preliminary Fragment to the Study of Law

fuentes/fragmento-preliminar/resumen.texto: Essay published by Alberdi in Buenos Aires in 1837, in the climate of the Salón Literario. Following Lerminier and the historical school, it holds that law must be studied as an expression of the life of each people and that Argentina needs a philosophy and laws of its own, not copied from Europe. It praises Rosas as a ruler who represented the people, a judgment Alberdi abandoned when he went into exile.

fuentes/fragmento-preliminar/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first philosophical text of the Generation of '37 and the starting point of Alberdi's legal thought, the author years later of the Bases.

fuentes/fragmento-preliminar/leer.0.titu.texto: In volume I of Alberdi's Obras completas (1886), on Internet Archive

fuentes/amalia/resumen.texto: Novel set in Buenos Aires in 1840. It opens with the Mazorca's ambush of a group of young men trying to flee to Montevideo; one of them, Eduardo Belgrano, wounded, takes refuge in Amalia's house, and the plot crosses the pursued with Rosas, Manuelita, María Josefa Ezcurra, Cuitiño and the regime's spies. It was published in installments in Montevideo from 1851 and completed in Buenos Aires in 1855.

fuentes/amalia/por_que_importa.texto: It is often considered the first major Argentine novel, and it fixed the literary image of the Mazorca and of the terror of 1840 from the viewpoint of its victims.

fuentes/manuela-rosas-marmol/resumen.texto: Biographical pamphlet by José Mármol on Rosas's daughter, published in Montevideo. It presents Manuelita sympathetically, as a young woman trapped in her father's regime and forced to serve him, while sharply criticizing Rosas.

fuentes/manuela-rosas-marmol/por_que_imp.texto: It contributed to the image of Manuelita as the kindly face of Rosismo, which later novels and biographies repeated.

fuentes/argiropolis/resumen.texto: Pamphlet published in Santiago de Chile in 1850 proposing the creation of the Confederated States of the Río de la Plata, with Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay, and a federal capital on Martín García island, called Argirópolis. It calls for a congress, a constitution and free navigation of the rivers, and is addressed largely to Urquiza as a possible head of that reorganization.

fuentes/argiropolis/por_que_importa.texto: It sets out the emigration's program for after Rosas, with the question of the rivers and of the capital at its center.

fuentes/argiropolis/leer.0.titulo.texto: Volume XIII of Sarmiento's Obras (1896), on Internet Archive

fuentes/recuerdos-de-provincia/resumen.texto: Autobiography and genealogy published by Sarmiento in Santiago de Chile in 1850, with portraits of colonial San Juan, of his mother Paula Albarracín and of his priest and lettered relatives, and the account of his own education. He wrote it in part to answer the attacks of the Rosist press against him.

fuentes/recuerdos-de-provincia/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the first autobiographies in Argentine literature and a source on provincial society at the end of the colonial period and the beginning of independence.

fuentes/viajes-sarmiento/titulo.texto: Travels in Europe, Africa and America

fuentes/viajes-sarmiento/resumen.texto: Letters from the journey Sarmiento made between 1845 and 1847, commissioned by the Chilean government, to study education systems: Montevideo, Rio de Janeiro, France, Spain, Algeria, Italy, Germany, England and the United States. It describes cities, customs and schools, and compares those countries with Spanish America.

fuentes/viajes-sarmiento/por_que_importa.texto: It shows the formation of Sarmiento's educational project and his admiration for the United States, and it is one of the great travel works of Spanish American literature.

fuentes/episodios-sangrientos-del-ano-18.texto: F. B. (initials of an unidentified author)

Pamphlet signed with the initials F. B. and published in Buenos Aires in 1856, after Rosas's fall, with accounts of the club of the Sociedad Popular Restauradora, the watchmen's barracks on Chacabuco Street, the society's founding, victims of 1840 and Rosas's house. Its author states that his aim is to recall “the criminal acts” committed under Rosas's administration.
It is an anti-Rosas testimony about the Mazorca, useful for its details about places and people but written with denunciatory intent and without declared sources.

fuentes/vindicacion-y-memorias-de-antoni.texto: Vindication and Memoirs of Don Antonino Reyes
Manuel Bilbao, on the recollections of Antonino Reyes

Book published by Manuel Bilbao in 1883 with the recollections of Antonino Reyes, Rosas's aide-de-camp and chief of the Santos Lugares prison, written to defend himself and to answer liberal histories. It includes his account of the execution of Camila O'Gorman and Ladislao Gutiérrez, which he witnessed up close.
It is one of the few testimonies written from inside Rosas's repressive apparatus; its exculpatory intent requires reading it with caution.

fuentes/steam-warfare-in-the-parana/resu.texto: Account by a British Navy officer who commanded a steamer in the Anglo-French squadron on the Paraná in 1846, during the escort of the merchant convoy after Obligado. It describes the fighting with the Mansilla batteries, navigation of the river, trade in Corrientes and Paraguay, and life on the Litoral.

fuentes/steam-warfare-in-the-parana/por_.texto: It is a firsthand testimony from the side of the interveners, useful for comparison with the Argentine reports.

fuentes/steam-warfare-in-the-parana/leer.texto: London edition of 1848 on Internet Archive

fuentes/two-thousand-miles-ride/titulo.texto: Two Thousand Miles' Ride through the Argentine Provinces

fuentes/two-thousand-miles-ride/resumen.texto: Account by the British merchant William MacCann of his horseback journeys through the province of Buenos Aires and the Litoral in the late 1840s: the estancias, the saladeros, the gauchos, the frontier with the Indigenous peoples, and daily life under Rosas's government, with a historical overview.

fuentes/two-thousand-miles-ride/por_que_.texto: It is one of the most detailed foreign descriptions of the Buenos Aires countryside in Rosas's time.

fuentes/two-thousand-miles-ride/leer.0.t.texto: London edition of 1853 on Internet Archive

fuentes/buenos-ayres-and-the-provinces/t.texto: Buenos Aires and the Provinces of the Río de la Plata

fuentes/buenos-ayres-and-the-provinces/r.texto: Description of Buenos Aires and the Río de la Plata provinces written by Woodbine Parish, who had served as British chargé d'affaires in Buenos Aires between 1825 and 1832. It gathers data on geography, population, trade, debt and production in each province, with information on the frontier and Patagonia.

fuentes/buenos-ayres-and-the-provinces/p.texto: It is one of the most complete foreign descriptions of the region in Rosas's early years, written by a diplomat with access to official sources.

fuentes/la-republica-argentina-37-anos-d.texto: The Argentine Republic Thirty-Seven Years after Its May Revolution

Pamphlet published by Alberdi in Valparaíso in 1847, from exile, which acknowledges that Rosas's government gave the country order, stability and an authority respected abroad, and holds that those conditions could serve as a basis for a future constitutional organization.
It shows that the liberal opposition was not homogeneous: its conciliatory tone was criticized by other emigrés and later cited by Rosas's defenders.

fuentes/montevideo-o-la-nueva-troya/resu.texto: Account of the siege of Montevideo written by Alexandre Dumas in 1850 with information supplied by Melchor Pacheco y Obes, minister of the Government of the Defense sent to Paris. It presents the city's defense as an epic and Rosas and Oribe as tyrants, to influence French opinion on the intervention.

fuentes/montevideo-o-la-nueva-troya/por_.texto: It is an example of the Montevideo government's propaganda campaign in Europe, and it gave the city the nickname “New Troy.”

fuentes/el-nacional-montevideo/resumen.texto: Montevideo newspaper that Andrés Lamas refounded in 1838 and in which Argentine emigrés of the Generation of '37 wrote, such as Miguel Cané, Juan Bautista Alberdi and José Rivera Indarte. There Rivera Indarte published much of the writing against Rosas that he gathered in Rosas and His Opponents (1843), and Lamas, in 1845, published his articles on Rosas's aggressions against Uruguayan independence.

fuentes/el-nacional-montevideo/por_que_i.texto: Before El Comercio del Plata, it was the main daily of the anti-Rosas emigration in Montevideo and one of the sources of its propaganda.

personas/rosas/resumen.texto: Estanciero and militia chief of the Buenos Aires countryside who governed Buenos Aires from 1829 to 1832 with extraordinary powers and from 1835 to 1852 with the full sum of public power, and who handled the foreign relations of the Argentine Confederation. His government pursued Unitarians and dissident Federalists with the police, the Mazorca, the confiscation of property and executions without trial; it faced the blockades of France and Great Britain and postponed the national constitution. Defeated at Caseros (1852), he lived in exile near Southampton until his death; liberal historians judged him a tyrant, and revisionists rehabilitated him as a defender of sovereignty.

personas/encarnacion-ezcurra/resumen.texto: Wife of Juan Manuel de Rosas from 1813. In 1833, while her husband led the Conquest of the Desert, she organized the Rosist Federalists, encouraged the Revolution of the Restorers against Governor Balcarce, and was at the origin of the Sociedad Popular Restauradora. She died in October 1838, and her funeral was a great political demonstration of Rosismo.

personas/manuelita-rosas/resumen.texto: Daughter of Juan Manuel de Rosas and Encarnación Ezcurra. After her mother's death she was the hostess of her father's residence and the intermediary to whom requests and pleas for clemency were addressed. She accompanied him into exile in 1852, married Máximo Terrero and lived in London until her death.

personas/lucio-norberto-mansilla/resumen.texto: Military officer of the independence and of the war with Brazil, married to Agustina Rosas, the governor's sister. He led the defense of the Vuelta de Obligado (1845), the attacks on the Anglo-French convoy on the Paraná in 1846 and the resistance to the passage of the Brazilian squadron at Tonelero (1851). He was the father of the writer Lucio V. Mansilla.

personas/felipe-arana/resumen.texto: Porteño lawyer, Rosas's minister of foreign relations from 1835 to 1852. He signed with France the Mackau convention (1840) and the Arana-Lepredour convention (1850), and with Great Britain the Arana-Southern convention (1849).

personas/juan-ramon-balcarce/resumen.texto: Military officer of the independence and leader of the non-Rosist Federalists, governor of Buenos Aires from December 1832. The Revolution of the Restorers forced him to resign on November 4, 1833, and he died in exile.

personas/juan-jose-viamonte/resumen.texto: Military officer of the independence, provisional governor of Buenos Aires in 1829 and again between November 1833 and June 1834, after the Revolution of the Restorers and under pressure from the Rosists. He died in exile in Montevideo.

personas/manuel-vicente-maza/resumen.texto: Federalist lawyer and friend of Rosas, interim governor of Buenos Aires (1834–1835), president of the Chamber of Representatives and of the Chamber of Justice. On June 27, 1839, once the conspiracy led by his son Ramón was uncovered, he was murdered in his office at the Legislature; the opposition and most historians attributed the crime to the Mazorca.

personas/ramon-maza/resumen.texto: Colonel of the Buenos Aires frontier who in 1839 led a conspiracy to overthrow Rosas, coordinated with Lavalle and with estancieros of the south. Betrayed, he was shot in prison without trial in the early hours of June 28, 1839, hours after his father's murder.

personas/pascual-echague/resumen.texto: Governor of Entre Ríos (1832–1841) and later of Santa Fe, an ally of Rosas. He defeated Berón de Astrada at Pago Largo (1839) and was defeated by Rivera at Cagancha (1839) and by Paz at Caaguazú (1841).

personas/angel-pacheco/resumen.texto: General of the independence and one of Rosas's main military leaders. He pursued Lavalle in 1840 and defeated Lamadrid at Rodeo del Medio (1841); on the eve of Caseros he gave up command of the Porteño army.

personas/mariano-maza/resumen.texto: Porteño military officer in Oribe's army during the campaign against the Northern Coalition. On his orders, the Catamarca governor José Cubas and Marco Avellaneda were executed in 1841; Avellaneda's throat was cut at Metán on October 3. After Caseros he lived in Montevideo, where he died.

personas/juan-bautista-thorne/resumen.texto: Naval officer born in New York who served the United Provinces and the Confederation. At Obligado (1845) he commanded the Manuelita battery, the last to resist upstream of the chains.

personas/martiniano-chilavert/resumen.texto: Artillery officer who first fought against Rosas, alongside Lavalle and Paz, and in 1851 switched to his army. He commanded the Rosist artillery at Caseros and, taken prisoner, was shot on Urquiza's orders on February 4, 1852.

personas/julian-gonzalez-salomon/resumen.texto: Porteño pulpero and militia colonel, president of the Sociedad Popular Restauradora, the club of Rosist Federalists that organized demonstrations, electoral lists and punishments against opponents.

personas/ciriaco-cuitino/resumen.texto: Merchant and Federalist alcalde born in Mendoza, police commissioner from 1830 and, with Andrés Parra, head of the police squads that acted as the armed arm of the Sociedad Popular Restauradora and were called the Mazorca. Publicly tried in December 1853 for the murders committed under Rosas, he was sentenced to death and shot together with Leandro Alén, and their bodies were exposed hanging in the Plaza de la Concepción.

personas/andres-parra/resumen.texto: Buenos Aires police commissioner who led, together with Ciriaco Cuitiño, one of the two special police and night-watch bodies that pursued Rosas's opponents and became known as the Mazorca.

personas/silverio-badia/resumen.texto: Police officer and member of the Mazorca. The decree of August 11, 1853 subjected him to ordinary justice for the crimes of Rosas's era; sentenced to death, he was executed in October 1853 and his body was exposed on the gallows.

personas/manuel-troncoso/resumen.texto: Police officer and member of the Mazorca, prosecuted with Badía under the decree of August 11, 1853. Sentenced to death, he was executed in October 1853 and his body was exposed on the gallows.

personas/fermin-suarez/resumen.texto: Member of the Mazorca prosecuted under the decree of August 11, 1853 and sentenced to death. He was executed at the end of October 1853 and his body was left exposed on the gallows.

personas/leandro-alen/resumen.texto: Pulpero of the Balvanera neighborhood and member of the Mazorca. Tried together with Ciriaco Cuitiño in December 1853, he was shot and his body was exposed hanging in the Plaza de la Concepción; his son, the future founder of the Unión Cívica Radical, Leandro N. Alem, changed the spelling of the surname.

personas/antonino-reyes/resumen.texto: Aide-de-camp and secretary to Rosas and chief of the prison at the Santos Lugares camp, where political prisoners, among them Camila O'Gorman and Ladislao Gutiérrez, were shot on the governor's written order. Prosecuted from August 1853 for those executions, he escaped from prison in June 1854 and had the charges against him dismissed in 1855; his recollections, published by Manuel Bilbao in 1883, are a testimony from within the regime.

personas/camila-ogorman/resumen.texto: Young woman from the Porteño upper class and a friend of Manuelita Rosas, who in December 1847 fled with the priest Ladislao Gutiérrez and settled with him in Goya (Corrientes), where they opened a school. Discovered in June 1848, they were shot without trial on Rosas's order at Santos Lugares on August 18, 1848.

personas/ladislao-gutierrez/resumen.texto: Priest from Tucumán, parish priest of El Socorro in Buenos Aires and a relative of the governor of Tucumán, Celedonio Gutiérrez. He fled with Camila O'Gorman in December 1847 and was shot with her at Santos Lugares on August 18, 1848.

personas/pedro-castelli/resumen.texto: Son of the May Revolution figure Juan José Castelli and one of the leaders of the revolution of the Libres del Sur (1839). After the defeat at Chascomús he was caught and killed by a Federalist squad, and his head was exposed on a pike in the plaza of Dolores.

personas/genaro-beron-de-astrada/resumen.texto: Governor of Corrientes who in 1839 rose against Rosas in alliance with Fructuoso Rivera. He died in the battle of Pago Largo on March 31, 1839.

personas/domingo-cullen/resumen.texto: Canary Islander merchant, minister of Estanislao López and governor of Santa Fe in 1838, upon the death of the latter. Accused by Rosas of negotiating with the French who were blockading the port, he took refuge in Santiago del Estero; Ibarra handed him over, and he was shot without trial on Rosas's orders on June 22, 1839, at the Vergara post station, just after crossing the Arroyo del Medio toward Buenos Aires.

personas/marco-avellaneda/nacimiento.lug.texto: San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca

personas/marco-avellaneda/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Catamarca, governor of Tucumán and civil chief of the Northern Coalition against Rosas. After the defeat at Famaillá he was handed over to Oribe, sentenced for treason, and had his throat cut in Metán on October 3, 1841; his head was impaled on a pike in the plaza of Tucumán. He was the father of President Nicolás Avellaneda.

personas/joaquin-madariaga/resumen.texto: Governor of Corrientes from 1843, who with his brother Juan sustained the Corrientes resistance against Rosas, allied with Paz and with Paraguay. He signed with Urquiza the Treaty of Alcaraz (1846), which Rosas rejected, and was defeated at Vences in November 1847.

personas/alejandro-heredia/resumen.texto: Governor of Tucumán (1832–1838) and protector of the northern provinces, an ally of Rosas, who led the war against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation. He was assassinated by a group of officers in November 1838.

personas/jose-felix-aldao/resumen.texto: Dominican friar who fought in the Army of the Andes and became the Federalist leader of Mendoza, governing from 1841 to 1845. He fought the Northern Coalition, and Sarmiento published a critical biography of him in 1845.

personas/joaquin-suarez/resumen.texto: Uruguayan politician, president of the Government of the Defense of Montevideo during the Great Siege (1843–1852), opposed to Oribe and Rosas.

personas/garibaldi/resumen.texto: Italian revolutionary who, in the Guerra Grande of Uruguay, commanded the flotilla of the Montevideo government and the Italian Legion. He was defeated by Brown at Costa Brava (1842), and in 1845 his forces, backed by the Anglo-French squadron, took and sacked Gualeguaychú. He returned to Italy in 1848 and became one of the leaders of Italian unification.

personas/pedro-de-angelis/resumen.texto: Neapolitan scholar who arrived in Buenos Aires in 1827 and became the main publicist of Rosas's government. He published the Colección de obras y documentos (Collection of Works and Documents, 1836–1837), the first major edition of sources on the history of the Río de la Plata, and directed the Archivo Americano (1843–1851), which defended Rosas's foreign policy in three languages.

personas/jose-rivera-indarte/resumen.texto: Poet from Córdoba who in the 1830s wrote verses in homage to Rosas and the Restorers and later became his opponent. Exiled in Montevideo, he wrote for El Nacional and published Rosas and His Opponents (1843), with the Tables of Blood and the article “It Is a Holy Deed to Kill Rosas.” He died in Santa Catarina (Brazil) in 1845.

personas/florencio-varela/resumen.texto: Unitarian lawyer and writer, brother of the poet Juan Cruz Varela, exiled in Montevideo during Rosas's government. In 1845 he founded El Comercio del Plata, the main opposition newspaper, where he defended free navigation of the rivers; he was assassinated in Montevideo on March 20, 1848.

personas/esteban-echeverria/resumen.texto: Porteño poet who brought Romanticism from Paris, author of Elvira (1832), Los consuelos (1834) and Rimas (1837), which includes “The Captive Woman.” In 1838 he founded the Asociación de la Joven Generación Argentina, whose creed he later published as Socialist Dogma, and he wrote “The Slaughterhouse.” He went into exile in Uruguay around 1840 and died poor in Montevideo in 1851.

personas/juan-maria-gutierrez/resumen.texto: Porteño writer and critic of the Generation of '37, of the Salón Literario and of the Asociación de Mayo. Exiled in Montevideo and Chile, he published the anthology América poética (1846); after Caseros he was a constituent member in 1853, minister of the Confederation and rector of the University of Buenos Aires, and in 1871 he made public Echeverría's “The Slaughterhouse.”

personas/vicente-fidel-lopez/resumen.texto: Son of Vicente López y Planes and member of the Generation of '37. Exiled in Chile, he taught and wrote the historical novel The Heretic's Bride; after Caseros he served as minister in Buenos Aires and later became a historian, author of a History of the Argentine Republic and a rival of Mitre in the debate over historical method.

personas/jose-marmol/resumen.texto: Porteño poet and novelist, imprisoned by Rosas's government in 1839 and exiled in Montevideo from 1840. He wrote verses against Rosas, the Songs of the Pilgrim, the pamphlet Manuela Rosas (1850) and the novel Amalia, published in installments in Montevideo from 1851. After Caseros he was a legislator and director of the Biblioteca Pública de Buenos Aires.

personas/marcos-sastre/resumen.texto: Bookseller and educator born in Montevideo, in whose Librería Argentina the Salón Literario of 1837 met. He later wrote El Tempe argentino (1858) and schoolbooks.

personas/andres-lamas/resumen.texto: Uruguayan writer and politician who founded in 1838, with the help of Miguel Cané, the newspaper El Iniciador, where the exiles of the Generation of '37 wrote. He was political chief of Montevideo during the siege and later a diplomat of the Government of the Defense in Rio de Janeiro.

personas/miguel-cane-padre/resumen.texto: Porteño writer and journalist exiled in Montevideo, contributor to Andrés Lamas's El Iniciador (1838) and member of the Generation of '37. He was the father of the writer Miguel Cané, author of Juvenilia.

personas/charles-hotham/resumen.texto: Captain of the British Navy who commanded the British division in the battle of Vuelta de Obligado (1845). He later became governor of the colony of Victoria, in Australia.

personas/francois-trehouart/resumen.texto: Officer of the French Navy who commanded the French division in the battle of Vuelta de Obligado (1845) and rose to admiral.

personas/baron-de-mackau/resumen.texto: French admiral sent to the Río de la Plata in 1840, who signed with Felipe Arana the convention of October 29, 1840, which ended the French blockade. He later served as minister of the navy under Louis Philippe.

personas/henry-southern/resumen.texto: British journalist and diplomat, minister in Buenos Aires, who signed with Felipe Arana the convention of November 24, 1849, which closed the conflict between Great Britain and the Confederation.

personas/andres-de-santa-cruz/resumen.texto: Military officer and president of Bolivia (1829–1839) who created the Peru-Bolivian Confederation in 1836. Chile and Rosas's Argentine Confederation declared war on it, and its defeat at Yungay (1839) dissolved the Confederation.

personas/tomas-guido/resumen.texto: Porteño military officer and diplomat, a collaborator of San Martín in the campaigns of Chile and Peru. He signed the Preliminary Peace Convention with Brazil in 1828 and from 1840 to 1851 represented Argentina before the Brazilian government, in the era of Rosas. After Caseros he worked with Urquiza and was vice president of the Senate of the Confederation in 1857.

personas/manuel-blanco-encalada/resumen.texto: Naval officer born in Buenos Aires who made his career in Chile: he was the first commander of Chile's squadron and provisional president in 1826. In the war against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation he led the first Chilean expedition, which signed with Andrés de Santa Cruz the Treaty of Paucarpata (November 17, 1837). The Chilean government disavowed it, and the war continued until Yungay (1839) with a second expedition, under Manuel Bulnes.

personas/mariano-roque-alonso/resumen.texto: Paraguayan militia officer who, on 9 February 1841, after the death of Francia, overthrew a triumvirate and was then consul together with Carlos Antonio López until 1844, although the government remained mostly in López's hands. During that consulate, in 1842, a congress ratified the independence of Paraguay, which Rosas did not recognize. He was born on 7 August 1791 in Capiatá, where he was baptized, or on 16 August 1792 in Ybytimí, depending on the source.

personas/jose-miguel-de-velasco/resumen.texto: Bolivian military man who had already been interim president in 1828 and 1829 and was vice president of Santa Cruz from 1829 to 1835; in the Peru-Bolivian Confederation war he was its chief of staff (1836–1839). After Yungay (January 1839) he rose against Santa Cruz, proclaimed the separation of Bolivia and was president until the 1841 coup, which exiled him to Argentina; he returned to the presidency in 1848 or 1849, depending on the source, and, overthrown by Belzú, went into exile there again.

personas/juan-francisco-giro/resumen.texto: Uruguayan politician of the Blanco party who, during the Guerra Grande, joined the government of Oribe at Cerrito, the ally of Rosas, and was a senator there from 1844. Once the war ended, the Assembly elected him president on 1 March 1852; he tried a policy of fusion between Blancos and Colorados. After the military mutiny of 18 July 1853 and the pressure of the anti-fusionist Colorado faction, on 24 September 1853 he took refuge with Berro at the French legation, and a triumvirate (Flores, Lavalleja and Rivera) took over the government.

personas/carlos-anaya/resumen.texto: Born in San Pedro (Buenos Aires), he followed Artigas, supported the Cruzada de los Treinta y Tres and was the author of the 1825 Ley de la Florida, which declared the Provincia Oriental del Brasil independent and united it with the Provincias Unidas. As president of the Senate he held the presidency of Uruguay between the end of Rivera's term (October 24, 1834) and Oribe's inauguration (March 1, 1835). A supporter of Oribe, he went into exile in Buenos Aires from 1838 to 1845 and later presided over the Court of Appeals of the Cerrito government.

personas/henry-stephen-fox/resumen.texto: British diplomat, minister in Buenos Aires from December 1831 until his transfer to Rio de Janeiro in June 1832; he later became minister in Washington. In his 1832 dispatch on the Falklands he set aside Palmerston's instruction to demand the revocation of Luis Vernet's authority, and warned that asserting British sovereignty could lead to disputes with the United States. London nevertheless decided on the occupation of 1833.

personas/john-mandeville/resumen.texto: British diplomat in Buenos Aires during much of Rosas's government (1836-1845); according to the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography he was born on January 17, 1773 (another source gives 1771) and died on March 16, 1861. In March 1838 he spoke with the commander of the French squadron, Leblanc, before the ultimatum of the French blockade, and in November 1842 he offered, with the Frenchman Lurde, a mediation in the Uruguayan war, making clear that rejecting it would mean a break with both powers. In 1845 he was replaced by Ouseley.

personas/william-gore-ouseley/resumen.texto: British diplomat who replaced Mandeville and, together with the Frenchman Deffaudis, demanded that Rosas cease hostilities against the government of Montevideo and withdraw the Confederation troops that were in Uruguay. Rosas rejected it; the diplomats issued an ultimatum on 21 July 1845 with a deadline of the 31st, and on that day Arana returned their passports. In August Brown's squadron was captured and on 18 September the blockade was declared. He was recalled to Europe after his mission clashed with Hood's (1846), and in 1850 he published Notes on the Slave Trade.

personas/john-hobart-caradoc/resumen.texto: British diplomat, second Baron Howden, who together with the Frenchman Colonna Walewski was received by Rosas in Buenos Aires on May 11, 1847, to negotiate an end to the blockade on the basis of what Hood had agreed, modified in Montevideo's favor. Rosas and Arana were willing to sign Hood's bases unchanged, and no agreement was reached. Howden ordered the lifting of the British blockade of the Uruguayan ports and went to Rio de Janeiro as minister. Great Britain withdrew from the blockade in mid-1847, and France continued until 1848.

personas/robert-gore/resumen.texto: British naval officer and Whig member of parliament, chargé d'affaires in Montevideo from 1846 and recognized by Rosas in Buenos Aires on 29 August 1851. After Caseros, Rosas took refuge at the British legation, and Gore, in agreement with the ship's captain, took him aboard the Locust, which would carry him into exile. In January 1853 he was expelled from Buenos Aires, during the siege by Hilario Lagos, for denouncing that the government was handing out weapons to British residents.

personas/gabriel-antonio-pereira/resumen.texto: Uruguayan politician, political nephew of Artigas and signatory of the Declaration of Independence of 1825. Between 24 October and 1 November 1838 he served as interim executive, elected by the Senate, after the resignation of Oribe and the trip of Carlos Anaya to Buenos Aires; he sat on the Assembly of Notables of the Government of Defense (1843) and was minister of government in 1847. He presided over Uruguay from 1856 to 1860. Some sources extend that first period to 1839; this entry limits it to the interim term.

personas/luis-vernet/resumen.texto: Hamburg-born merchant of French descent, appointed on June 10, 1829, by the Buenos Aires government as political and military commander of the Falkland Islands, where he founded a colony at Puerto Soledad. Argentina considers him its first commander on the islands. In July 1831, under Rosas's first government, his second-in-command, Matthew Brisbane, captured three American fishing vessels for violating its fishing regulations; in December of that year the USS Lexington attacked the colony. After the British occupation of January 1833 he could not return to the islands, and he sought compensation from the United States and Great Britain until his death.

hechos/colorados-del-monte/resumen.texto: Rosas organized at his Los Cerrillos estancia, in San Miguel del Monte, a company of cavalry militia, later a regiment, to fight Indigenous peoples and cattle rustlers on the frontier. With these “Colorados del Monte” he intervened in the anarchy of 1820 and in October of that year suppressed in Buenos Aires the uprising of Manuel Pagola against Governor Martín Rodríguez, which gave him political prestige.

hechos/primer-gobierno-de-rosas/resumen.texto: In December 1829, after defeating Lavalle, Rosas was elected governor of Buenos Aires by the Chamber of Representatives, with the title of Restorer of the Laws and extraordinary powers. He governed by decree, signed the Federal Pact (1831), suppressed the Unitarian newspapers, subjected the press to prior permission and imposed the punzó badge on military officers and public employees (1832). At the end of his term he rejected reelection without extraordinary powers and in December 1832 handed the government to Juan Ramón Balcarce.

hechos/fusilamientos-de-san-nicolas-1831.texto: Executions at San Nicolás de los Arroyos

On October 16, 1831, during the war against José María Paz's Interior League, officers of Paz's army taken prisoner were shot without trial at San Nicolás de los Arroyos on Rosas's orders, among them Colonel Luis Videla, governor of San Luis. The event was one of the charges in the trial of Rosas, in which witnesses to the execution testified.

hechos/divisa-punzo/resumen.texto: On February 3, 1832, Rosas made the punzó badge, a red ribbon with Federalist slogans, mandatory for military officers and public employees. Over the years its use spread to the entire population, and not wearing it could bring detention or punishment. Official documents and La Gaceta Mercantil carried the header “Long live the Argentine Confederation! Death to the savage Unitarians!”, which Urquiza's Pronunciamiento replaced in 1851 with “Death to the enemies of the National Organization!”

hechos/censura-de-la-prensa-1832/resumen.texto: Using his extraordinary powers, Rosas suspended, during his first government, the newspapers that had supported Lavalle, and by a decree of February 1832 he prohibited any printing press from operating or any newspaper from being published without prior government permission, with fines and imprisonment for press offenses. From then on the Buenos Aires press was reduced to pro-government newspapers such as La Gaceta Mercantil, and the opposition was published in Montevideo, Chile and Bolivia.

hechos/ocupacion-britanica-de-las-malvin.texto: British Occupation of the Falkland Islands

In early January 1833, during the government of Juan Ramón Balcarce, the British corvette Clio arrived at Puerto Soledad and ordered the Buenos Aires garrison to withdraw, and Great Britain took possession of the islands. The Buenos Aires government protested, and the claim remained present in Rosas's diplomacy with Great Britain.

hechos/revolucion-de-los-restauradores/r.texto: On October 11, 1833, a crowd of Rosas's Federalists prevented, in Buenos Aires, the trial of a newspaper called El Restaurador de las Leyes and gathered armed in Barracas with military and police chiefs. Encarnación Ezcurra, while Rosas was on the desert campaign, coordinated her husband's supporters. Governor Juan Ramón Balcarce, a non-Rosas Federalist, resigned on November 4; he was replaced by Juan José Viamonte, and many Federalists opposed to Rosas, the so-called lomos negros, emigrated to Montevideo.

hechos/sociedad-popular-restauradora/res.texto: Club of Rosista Federalists made up of pulperos (general-store keepers), merchants, artisans and militia officers, presided over by Julián González Salomón, organized between 1832 and 1833 under the impulse of Encarnación Ezcurra. It organized demonstrations, electoral lists and punishments against the homes of opponents, and over the years it added estancia owners and generals. Its armed squads were called the Mazorca; sources place its dissolution between 1843 and 1846.

hechos/la-mazorca/resumen.texto: Name given to the police squads that acted as the armed wing of the Sociedad Popular Restauradora, led by the police commissioners Ciriaco Cuitiño and Andrés Parra, with members such as Silverio Badía, Manuel Troncoso, Fermín Suárez and Leandro Alén. Its first known action was the shooting of April 29, 1834, against the homes of former minister Manuel José García and deputy Pedro Pablo Vidal; in 1840 and 1842 it slit the throats of opponents and suspects, looted homes and monitored the use of the punzó badge, and Rosas halted each wave of violence with an order. At the 1853 trials the accused argued that they had obeyed Rosas's orders; the opposition in exile presented the Mazorca as a machine of extermination, revisionism as excesses by partisans, and historians such as John Lynch as an instrument of terror controlled by the governor himself. Gabriel Di Meglio (2007) counted about twenty victims of the Mazorca in the city in each of the waves of 1840 and 1842, excluding executions ordered in writing, and Lynch estimated some 2,000 victims of the repression over the whole period.

hechos/suma-del-poder-publico-y-plebisci.texto: The Grant of Full Public Power and the 1835 Plebiscite

After the assassination of Facundo Quiroga at Barranca Yaco, the Chamber of Representatives of Buenos Aires elected Rosas governor for five years on March 7, 1835, and granted him “the full sum of public power,” with the sole obligation to defend the Catholic religion and the Federal cause. At Rosas's request, the city's inhabitants voted from March 26 to 28: more than 9,000 votes in favor and fewer than ten against, according to the counts cited by historians, whose figures vary among authors. He took office on April 13, 1835.

hechos/segundo-gobierno-de-rosas/resumen.texto: Rosas governed Buenos Aires from April 13, 1835, until Caseros with the full sum of public power, renewed by the Chamber of Representatives, and with control of foreign relations and of the Confederation's war, delegated by the other provinces; each year he presented his resignation and the Chamber rejected it. He postponed the constitution and the congress foreseen in the Federal Pact, persecuted opponents through the police, the Mazorca, censorship and the confiscation of property, and kept customs and river navigation under Buenos Aires control. His defenders stress domestic order and resistance to France and Great Britain; his critics stress the dictatorship and the terror.

hechos/sancion-de-la-ley-de-aduana-1835/.texto: On December 18, 1835, Rosas promulgated a customs law that raised import duties on products competing with domestic ones, prohibited the entry of some, such as hardware and candles, and prohibited foreign wheat and flour when the local price was low. It responded to the demands of the provinces against Buenos Aires' free trade, raised by Pedro Ferré since 1830, but Buenos Aires remained the only overseas customs house and kept its revenue. Revisionism presented it as a national protectionist policy; historians such as Miron Burgin and José Carlos Chiaramonte explain it as a fiscal and political compromise, of limited scope and applied flexibly in the following years.

hechos/los-jesuitas-bajo-rosas/titulo.texto: Return and Second Expulsion of the Jesuits

hechos/los-jesuitas-bajo-rosas/resumen.texto: In 1836 Rosas authorized the return of the Society of Jesus, expelled from the Spanish dominions in 1767, and returned to it the church and college of San Ignacio in Buenos Aires. The Jesuits refused to publicly support the government, as the clergy was required to do, and the conflict ended with their departure from Buenos Aires and their expulsion in 1843; many settled in Montevideo and in other countries.

hechos/salon-literario/resumen.texto: In June 1837 young men from Buenos Aires and the interior, among them Esteban Echeverría, Juan Bautista Alberdi, Juan María Gutiérrez and Vicente Fidel López, began to meet at Marcos Sastre's Librería Argentina in a reading and discussion salon. They sought a national culture distinct from the Spanish one and debated the French Romantic and socialist writers. Some still hoped Rosas would favor it, but given the government's distrust the salon closed in 1838.

hechos/asociacion-de-mayo/titulo.texto: Asociación de la Joven Generación Argentina

hechos/asociacion-de-mayo/resumen.texto: Secret society founded by Esteban Echeverría in mid-1838, later known as the Asociación de Mayo, which brought together young men from the Salón Literario under a creed of “symbolic words” written by him. Several of its members took part in the conspiracy of 1839, and almost all of them ended in exile, from where they spread their ideas in Montevideo, Chile and Bolivia.

hechos/guerra-contra-la-confederacion-pe.texto: In 1837 Rosas declared war on Andrés de Santa Cruz's Peru-Bolivian Confederation, which gave refuge to exiled Unitarians and had influence in northern Argentina, thus joining the war that Chile was waging against it. The army of the north, under Alejandro Heredia, played a minor role and failed to advance; the Confederation dissolved after the Chilean victory at Yungay in January 1839.

hechos/bloqueo-frances-1838/titulo.texto: French Blockade of the Río de la Plata

hechos/bloqueo-frances-1838/resumen.texto: On March 28, 1838, the French squadron under Rear Admiral Leblanc declared the blockade of Buenos Aires and of the ports of the Confederation. France demanded for its citizens exemption from the militia service that the British had been subject to since 1825, and reparations for damages, among them the imprisonment of the lithographer César Hipólito Bacle. The French seized Martín García island and supported Rivera, the Corrientes forces and Lavalle; the blockade caused customs revenues and the province's trade to fall until the convention of October 29, 1840.

hechos/toma-de-martin-garcia-1838/resume.texto: On October 11, 1838, French forces, with allied troops of Fructuoso Rivera, landed on Martín García island, defended by a small garrison under Jerónimo Costa, which surrendered after resisting. France used it as a base during the blockade and returned it under the convention of 1840.

hechos/naciones-africanas-de-buenos-aire.texto: The African Nations of Buenos Aires in the Rosas Era

In Rosas's time, Africans and Afro-Porteños of Buenos Aires, both free and enslaved, organized themselves into “nations” according to their origin, such as Congo, Mozambique or Benguela, with their own headquarters where they held candombes. Rosas, his wife and his daughter visited those festivities; many Afro-Porteños served in the Federalist militias, and the police monitored and regulated the nations. In 1839 the government signed a treaty with Great Britain to suppress the slave trade, and slavery was not abolished until the Constitution of 1853. Opposition literature, such as “The Slaughterhouse” and Amalia, presented Black Federalists as part of the Rosista plebs.

hechos/fusilamiento-de-domingo-cullen/re.texto: Former governor of Santa Fe Domingo Cullen, accused by Rosas of negotiating with the French who were blockading the Río de la Plata, was handed over by the governor of Santiago del Estero, Juan Felipe Ibarra, and shot without trial on Rosas's orders on June 22, 1839, at the Vergara post station, just after crossing the Arroyo del Medio, the boundary between Santa Fe and Buenos Aires. The case opened against Rosas in 1857 included him among its charges.

hechos/batalla-de-pago-largo/lugar.texto: Arroyo Pago Largo, south of Curuzú Cuatiá

hechos/batalla-de-pago-largo/resumen.texto: On March 31, 1839, the Entre Ríos army of Pascual Echagüe, Rosas's ally, defeated the forces of Corrientes, which had risen against Rosas in alliance with Fructuoso Rivera. Governor Genaro Berón de Astrada died in the battle. According to the accounts of the defeated recorded by historiography, hundreds of prisoners had their throats slit after the combat; the figures cited, of up to 800, have no precise documentary record.

hechos/conspiracion-de-maza/resumen.texto: In 1839 Colonel Ramón Maza and young men from Buenos Aires, several of them members of the Asociación de Mayo, prepared an uprising against Rosas, coordinated with Lavalle's invasion and with the southern estancieros. Denounced on June 26, the conspiracy was disarmed: on June 27 Manuel Vicente Maza, president of the Chamber of Representatives and the colonel's father, was murdered in his office at the Legislature, and on the 28th Ramón Maza was shot in jail without trial. The opposition and most historians attributed the murder to the Mazorca; Adolfo Saldías argued, on the other hand, that the conspirators themselves had killed him to keep the organization from being discovered.

hechos/libres-del-sur/titulo.texto: Revolution of the Libres del Sur

hechos/libres-del-sur/resumen.texto: Uprising of estancieros in the south of Buenos Aires province, harmed by the French blockade and by the government's fiscal demands, which broke out in Dolores on October 29, 1839, under Pedro Castelli, Ambrosio Crámer and Manuel Rico, awaiting the landing of Lavalle. Government forces under Prudencio Rosas and Nicolás Granada defeated them at Chascomús on November 7; Crámer died in the fighting, and Castelli was caught and killed, and his head was displayed on a pike in the plaza of Dolores. The property of those involved was attached.

hechos/campana-de-lavalle/resumen.texto: With support from the French squadron, Juan Lavalle landed in Entre Ríos in September 1839, won at Yeruá and, with an army formed in Corrientes, advanced in 1840 to the outskirts of Buenos Aires. Without the uprising he expected in the Buenos Aires countryside, he withdrew in September 1840 toward the interior, was defeated by Oribe at Quebracho Herrado and Famaillá, and died in Jujuy in October 1841. The Federalists reproached him for his alliance with France against the government of his own country, and the exile community itself debated it.

hechos/batalla-de-cagancha/resumen.texto: On December 29, 1839, Fructuoso Rivera defeated at Cagancha, in Uruguay, the army of Pascual Echagüe that Rosas had sent to invade the Eastern State in support of Manuel Oribe. The victory sustained Rivera's government in Montevideo for several years.

hechos/coalicion-del-norte/resumen.texto: On April 7, 1840, the Chamber of Representatives of Tucumán repudiated Rosas as the agent in charge of foreign relations, and Salta, Catamarca, La Rioja and Jujuy formed with it a league against him, with Tomás Brizuela as director of the war and Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid and Lavalle as military leaders. Their governments invoked the need for a constitution. The armies of Oribe and Pacheco destroyed it in 1841, and many of its leaders were executed after surrendering or being captured, among them Marco Avellaneda, the governor of Catamarca José Cubas and General Mariano Acha.

hechos/decreto-de-confiscacion/titulo.texto: Seizure of the Property of the Unitarians

hechos/decreto-de-confiscacion/resumen.texto: On September 16, 1840, with Lavalle still in the province, Rosas decreed that the property of the “savage Unitarians” was set aside to repair the damage of the invasion and to reward the government's defenders, and prohibited selling or mortgaging it. Seizures followed of estancias, houses and cattle belonging to opponents and suspects, administered by the state or handed over to supporters; after Caseros many owners claimed their return.

hechos/terror-de-1840/resumen.texto: After Lavalle withdrew from the outskirts of Buenos Aires in September 1840, the Mazorca roamed the city for weeks: it slit the throats of opponents and suspects, looted homes and destroyed whatever was sky blue or green, colors associated with the Unitarians. At the end of October Rosas ordered the violence stopped on pain of death, and it stopped. Rivera Indarte recounted it as a great massacre in Rosas and His Opponents; the historian Gabriel Di Meglio (2007), who separates the deaths attributable to the Mazorca, counts about twenty in the city, not including the countryside or those shot by written order, and revisionism uses figures like these to present the terror as an exceptional excess.

hechos/terror-de-1842/resumen.texto: In April 1842, in the midst of the war against Rivera and the Corrientes forces, the Mazorca again slit the throats of opponents and looted homes in Buenos Aires for several days. As in 1840, Rosas ended the wave of violence with an order. Rivera Indarte devoted a chapter of Rosas and His Opponents to the “April 1842 massacres,” and Gabriel Di Meglio (2007) counts about twenty victims in the city.

hechos/batalla-de-quebracho-herrado/resu.texto: On November 28, 1840, Manuel Oribe's Federalist army defeated Juan Lavalle at Quebracho Herrado, in eastern Córdoba, as he retreated north after his campaign against Buenos Aires. It was the beginning of the collapse of the Northern Coalition.

hechos/batalla-de-famailla/resumen.texto: On September 19, 1841, Oribe defeated Lavalle at Famaillá (Tucumán) and destroyed the last army of the Northern Coalition. In the following weeks several of its leaders were captured and executed, among them Marco Avellaneda.

hechos/batalla-de-rodeo-del-medio/resume.texto: On September 24, 1841, Ángel Pacheco defeated Gregorio Aráoz de Lamadrid's army near Mendoza, the last force of the Northern Coalition in Cuyo. Lamadrid and the remnants of his army crossed the Andes into Chile.

hechos/ejecucion-de-marco-avellaneda/res.texto: Marco Avellaneda, civil chief of the Northern Coalition, was handed over to Oribe by an officer of his escort while fleeing after Famaillá. Sentenced for treason, he had his throat cut in Metán (Salta) on October 3, 1841, by order of Colonel Mariano Maza, and his head was impaled on a pike in the plaza of Tucumán.

hechos/muerte-de-lavalle/resumen.texto: On October 9, 1841, during his retreat after Famaillá, Juan Lavalle was shot dead in a house in San Salvador de Jujuy, in a gunfight with a Federalist party. His officers carried the body to Bolivia so that it would not be decapitated, and his remains returned to Buenos Aires in 1861.

hechos/batalla-de-caaguazu/resumen.texto: On November 28, 1841, General José María Paz, at the head of the Corrientes army, defeated Pascual Echagüe at Caaguazú. It was the greatest military victory of Rosas's opponents, but the rivalries among Paz, Governor Pedro Ferré and Rivera prevented them from taking advantage of it.

hechos/combate-de-costa-brava/resumen.texto: Naval battle fought in August 1842 on the Paraná River, in which the Confederation's squadron under Guillermo Brown defeated the flotilla of the Montevideo government led by Giuseppe Garibaldi, who had his ships set on fire so they would not be surrendered.

hechos/batalla-de-arroyo-grande/resumen.texto: On December 6, 1842, the Confederation army under Manuel Oribe defeated Fructuoso Rivera and his Corrientes allies at Arroyo Grande, in Entre Ríos. The opposition denounced the slaughter of prisoners after the battle; Oribe then moved into Uruguay, and in February 1843 began the siege of Montevideo.

hechos/guerra-grande/resumen.texto: Uruguayan civil war between the Blanco party of Manuel Oribe, backed by Rosas, and the Colorado party of Fructuoso Rivera, backed by exiled Argentine Unitarians, by France and Great Britain and, at the end, by Brazil. The Argentine Confederation intervened with its armies and its squadron, and the war merged with the Argentine civil war and with the European blockades. It ended on October 8, 1851, when Oribe made a pact with Urquiza under the formula that there would be neither losers nor winners.

hechos/sitio-grande-de-montevideo/resume.texto: From February 16, 1843, Oribe's army, with troops of the Argentine Confederation, besieged Montevideo, defended by the Government of the Defense of Joaquín Suárez, by legions of immigrants and exiles and, from the river, by the British and French fleets. Oribe set up his own government at the Cerrito, and the besieged city, where the Argentine exile newspapers were published, was called “the new Troy” by Alexandre Dumas. The siege ended in October 1851.

hechos/batalla-de-india-muerta/resumen.texto: On March 27, 1845, Justo José de Urquiza, at the head of a Confederation army, defeated Fructuoso Rivera at India Muerta, in eastern Uruguay, leaving the government of Montevideo without a field army.

hechos/bloqueo-anglofrances/titulo.texto: Anglo-French Blockade of the Río de la Plata

hechos/bloqueo-anglofrances/resumen.texto: Great Britain and France, which demanded the withdrawal of Argentine troops from Uruguay and the opening of the rivers to trade, captured Brown's squadron off Montevideo in August 1845, and on September 18 declared the blockade of the Confederation's ports. Great Britain lifted it in July 1847 and France in 1848, and peace was signed with the Arana–Southern (1849) and Arana–Lepredour (1850) treaties. The intervention did not achieve its aims: Confederation troops remained in Uruguay until 1851, and direct trade via the Paraná failed. Corrientes and Paraguay, allied against Rosas, for their part demanded the right to trade on the rivers without passing through Buenos Aires, and Rosas's supporters and revisionism celebrated the outcome as a victorious defense of sovereignty.

hechos/saqueo-de-gualeguaychu/resumen.texto: In September 1845, during the expedition of the Anglo-French squadron and the Montevideo flotilla up the Uruguay River, the forces of Giuseppe Garibaldi took Gualeguaychú and sacked it. The episode was used by the Rosista press against the intervention and against the exiles allied with it.

hechos/vuelta-de-obligado/resumen.texto: On November 20, 1845, eleven British and French warships, several of them steamships, attacked the four batteries of Lucio N. Mansilla at Vuelta de Obligado and the three chains stretched across 24 lighters that closed the Paraná. After a day of combat they cut the chains, landed and took the batteries. Estimates of Argentine casualties range from about 150 to 250 dead and from 90 to 400 wounded, depending on the account, and those of the allies from 26 to 28 dead and 86 to 95 wounded. Of the more than 90 merchant ships waiting, about 50 went up the river under escort, but the attacks from the shore and the lack of buyers made the venture fail. In 1849 and 1850 Great Britain and France signed treaties that recognized navigation of the Paraná as interior to the Confederation; Corrientes and Paraguay, then allied against Rosas, demanded to trade on the river without passing through the Buenos Aires customs house. Revisionism made the battle a symbol of sovereignty: the historian José María Rosa proposed the Día de la Soberanía Nacional (National Sovereignty Day), established by law in 1974 and a national holiday since 2010.

hechos/combate-de-san-lorenzo-1846/resum.texto: On January 16, 1846, Lucio N. Mansilla's batteries, placed on the bluffs of San Lorenzo on the Paraná, attacked ships of the Anglo-French squadron escorting the merchant convoy upriver, in a series of harassing attacks that followed Obligado.

hechos/batalla-de-punta-quebracho/resume.texto: On June 4, 1846, Mansilla attacked from the bluffs of Punta Quebracho, north of Rosario, the Anglo-French convoy coming down the Paraná on its return from Corrientes. According to historiography, the convoy lost six merchant ships, set on fire by artillery or by their crews when they ran aground, and two warships were damaged, with very few Argentine casualties.

hechos/batalla-de-vences/lugar.texto: Rincón de Vences (San Luis del Palmar, Corrientes)

hechos/batalla-de-vences/resumen.texto: On November 27, 1847, Urquiza defeated at Vences the army of the governor of Corrientes, Joaquín Madariaga, the last province in revolt against Rosas. Rosas had rejected in 1846 the Treaty of Alcaraz, with which Urquiza and the Madariagas had made peace, and after Vences the Confederation was left without armed opponents in its territory.

hechos/asesinato-de-florencio-varela/res.texto: On March 20, 1848, Florencio Varela, founder of El Comercio del Plata, was stabbed at the door of his home in Montevideo by Andrés Cabrera. Opponents accused Oribe and Rosas of having ordered it; the responsibility of those who ordered it was never proven.

hechos/fusilamiento-de-camila-ogorman/ti.texto: Execution of Camila O'Gorman and Ladislao Gutiérrez

hechos/fusilamiento-de-camila-ogorman/re.texto: In December 1847 Camila O'Gorman and the priest Ladislao Gutiérrez fled Buenos Aires and lived in Goya under false names. From Chile, Sarmiento used the escape to accuse the government of corrupting morals; the young woman's father asked Rosas to rescue her, and members of the clergy and jurists demanded an exemplary punishment. Discovered in June 1848, they were ordered shot without trial by Rosas at Santos Lugares, a sentence carried out on August 18, although Camila had declared that she was pregnant. The same opposition that had called for punishment condemned the execution as proof of cruelty, and Rosas later wrote that no one had advised him and that the responsibility was his alone. For John Lynch, the clergy and lawyers urged severity, but the sentence was Rosas's exclusive responsibility.

hechos/firma-del-tratado-arana-southern/.texto: On November 24, 1849, Felipe Arana and the British minister Henry Southern signed the convention that re-established relations between the Confederation and Great Britain. The British returned Martín García and the captured ships, saluted the Argentine flag, and recognized navigation of the Paraná as interior to the Confederation; the convention was ratified in 1850.

hechos/firma-de-la-convencion-arana-lepr.texto: On August 31, 1850, Felipe Arana and French Admiral Lepredour signed the convention that closed the French intervention on terms similar to those of the treaty with Great Britain. The French Assembly delayed its ratification and never approved it.
