hechos/pronunciamiento-de-urquiza-1851/r.texto: On May 1, 1851, Urquiza, governor of Entre Ríos, decreed that his province accepted the resignation that Rosas submitted each year and resumed control of its foreign relations and of peace and war, until a national assembly constituted the Republic; Corrientes followed. Behind it stood the constitution postponed since the Federal Pact of 1831, Buenos Aires' control of customs and river navigation, which harmed Entre Ríos trade, and the imminent war between Rosas and Brazil. Revisionism judged it a betrayal in alliance with the Empire, and liberal historiography the beginning of national organization.

hechos/alianza-contra-rosas-1851/titulo.texto: Alliance of Entre Ríos, Brazil and Uruguay

hechos/alianza-contra-rosas-1851/resumen.texto: On May 29, 1851, Entre Ríos, the Empire of Brazil and the government of Montevideo signed an alliance to expel Oribe from Uruguay; in October he made a pact with Urquiza and lifted the siege. Rosas declared war on Brazil in August, and on November 21 a new treaty with Corrientes directed the alliance against his government, with a loan and a Brazilian division for Urquiza's army. In October 1851 the government of Montevideo also signed boundary, trade and loan treaties with Brazil, among others.

hechos/batalla-del-tonelero-1851/resumen.texto: On December 17, 1851, a Brazilian naval division of seven ships forced passage of the Paraná off El Tonelero, in the Ramallo district, under fire from Lucio N. Mansilla's batteries, to transport troops to join Urquiza's army.

hechos/batalla-de-caseros/resumen.texto: On February 3, 1852, Urquiza's Grand Army, with troops from Entre Ríos, Corrientes and Buenos Aires, a Brazilian division and a Uruguayan one, defeated Rosas's army on the fields of Caseros, west of Buenos Aires. The two armies were of similar size, with more than twenty thousand men on each side according to estimates. Rosas signed his resignation and took refuge at the British legation. After the battle Urquiza had Colonel Martiniano Chilavert, chief of Rosas's artillery, shot, along with the soldiers of the Aquino regiment, who had defected to Rosas after killing their commander. The battle ended Rosas's government and opened the way to the San Nicolás Agreement and the Constitution of 1853.

hechos/exilio-de-rosas/resumen.texto: After Caseros Rosas sailed with his daughter Manuelita on a British ship and settled in England, where he leased a farm in Swaythling, near Southampton. Buenos Aires confiscated his property and tried him in absentia, and Urquiza, by then reconciled with him, sent him financial aid. He died on March 14, 1877, and was buried in Southampton. His remains were repatriated in 1989 and placed in the Recoleta cemetery, in an act that the government of the time presented as national reconciliation.

hechos/ejecucion-de-los-mazorqueros-1853.texto: Trial and Execution of the Mazorqueros

By decree of August 11, 1853, the government of Buenos Aires referred Silverio Badía, Manuel Troncoso, Antonino Reyes, Fermín Suárez, Estanislao Porto, Manuel Gervasio López, Leandro Alén, Ciriaco Cuitiño and others accused of the Mazorca's crimes to the ordinary courts. The defense argued that they had obeyed orders from Rosas, whom no one could disobey, and the courts sentenced several of them to death. Badía and Troncoso were executed in mid-October, Suárez at the end of that month, and Cuitiño and Alén on December 29, 1853; their bodies were displayed hanging. Reyes escaped from jail in June 1854 and was cleared of charges in 1855.

hechos/juicio-a-rosas/resumen.texto: On July 29, 1857, the Legislature of the State of Buenos Aires declared Rosas “guilty of treason against the fatherland for the bloody tyranny he exercised over the people” and subjected him to the ordinary courts for the common crimes of his government. Prosecutor Emilio Agrelo charged him in 1859, with charges such as the executions at San Nicolás (1831) and of Domingo Cullen (1839). On April 17, 1861, Judge Sixto Villegas sentenced him in absentia “to the ordinary penalty of death, with the qualification of treachery,” to restore what he had stolen and to be executed in Palermo; the Superior Tribunal confirmed the sentence. The sentence was never carried out because Rosas lived in England, and revisionism considered it a political trial by the victors.

hechos/darwin-visita-a-rosas/resumen.texto: In August 1833, during the voyage of the Beagle, Charles Darwin visited Rosas at his camp on the Colorado River, in the midst of the campaign against Indigenous peoples, and obtained from him a pass to travel across the pampas to Buenos Aires. In his diary he described Rosas as a man of extraordinary character and enormous influence over the gauchos, and recorded the violence of the campaign, including the massacre of captive Indigenous women.

hechos/emigracion-antirrosista/resumen.texto: During Rosas's governments, Unitarians, dissident Federalists and young members of the Generation of '37 emigrated, mainly to Montevideo, Chile and Bolivia. In Montevideo they published El Iniciador, El Nacional and El Comercio del Plata and formed an Argentine Commission that allied itself with France, Rivera and Lavalle. In Chile, Sarmiento, Alberdi and Vicente Fidel López wrote in the local press and published works such as Facundo (1845), the Bases (1852) and Argirópolis (1850). From exile they drafted much of the program of national organization that followed Caseros.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-escuela-de-precep.texto: Founding of the Escuela de Preceptores de Santiago

In 1842 the Chilean government of Manuel Bulnes, with Manuel Montt as minister of Public Instruction, founded in Santiago the Escuela de Preceptores, one of the first normal schools in the Americas, and placed the Argentine exile Domingo Faustino Sarmiento in charge of it. His studies for that post took him to travel through Europe and the United States between 1845 and 1847.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-ch.texto: Founding of the University of Chile

The University of Chile was created by law in November 1842 and installed in September 1843, with Andrés Bello as rector. Its faculties brought together Chilean intellectuals and Argentine émigrés of the Rosas era.

hechos/asesinato-de-alejandro-heredia/re.texto: On November 12, 1838, the governor of Tucumán, Alejandro Heredia, an ally of Rosas and leader of the war against the Peru-Bolivian Confederation, was assassinated at Lules by a group of officers. His death opened the way in the north to the governments that in 1840 formed the Northern Coalition.

hechos/batalla-de-angaco/resumen.texto: On August 16, 1841, forces of the Northern Coalition under Mariano Acha defeated those of José Félix Aldao at Angaco, north of San Juan. The victory was short-lived: shortly afterward the Federalists retook San Juan, captured Acha and executed him.

hechos/batalla-de-laguna-limpia/resumen.texto: On February 4, 1846, Urquiza defeated at Laguna Limpia, in southwest Corrientes, the advance columns of the Corrientes army and captured its leader, Juan Madariaga, the governor's brother. The capture opened the negotiations that led to the Treaty of Alcaraz.

hechos/rosas-y-la-independencia-del-para.texto: In 1842 a Paraguayan congress ratified the country's independence. Rosas refused to recognize it, because he considered Paraguay part of the Confederation, and kept control of navigation on the Paraná, the outlet for its trade. Paraguay allied in 1845 with Corrientes against Rosas, and its independence was recognized by Urquiza's government in 1852, after Caseros.

hechos/combate-del-tonelero-1846/resumen.texto: At the Tonelero crossing, opposite the present-day Ramallo district, Lucio N. Mansilla's batteries fired on the Anglo-French squadron and the merchant convoy as they went up the Paraná after Obligado, in January 1846, and again on their return, in mid-year. In both cases the ships forced the passage. Together with San Lorenzo and Punta Quebracho, they were part of the attacks from the shore that followed Obligado.

hechos/supresion-de-la-ensenanza-gratuit.texto: Suppression of Free Education in Buenos Aires

In 1838, with customs revenues falling because of the French blockade and war expenses, Rosas's government cancelled most of the education budget: it abolished free instruction and stopped paying the salaries of university professors. The University of Buenos Aires and the preparatory studies college continued to operate with fees charged to students, with far fewer professors and students.

hechos/guerra-platina/resumen.texto: A war between the Argentine Confederation, whose foreign relations Rosas managed, and an alliance of the Empire of Brazil, the Colorado government of Montevideo, and the provinces of Entre Ríos, governed by Urquiza, and Corrientes, governed by Benjamín Virasoro. In Argentina's internal politics it began with Urquiza's Pronouncement of May 1, 1851, and the alliance of May 29. Manuel Oribe, the Blanco leader and ally of Rosas, had been besieging Montevideo for years; Rosas declared war on Brazil on August 18, 1851, the Brazilian army entered Uruguay in September, Oribe surrendered in October, and the war ended with the allied victory at Caseros on February 3, 1852. It was part of a decades-long dispute between the Confederation and Brazil over influence in Uruguay and Paraguay and over supremacy on the Plate; Paraguay signed a defensive alliance with Brazil but did not send troops.

hechos/batalla-de-carpinteria/resumen.texto: On 19 September 1836 the army loyal to President Manuel Oribe, together with Lavalleja, defeated at the Carpintería stream, in Durazno, the rebellion of Fructuoso Rivera, who was allied with the Unitarian exiles under Juan Lavalle. Rivera fled to Brazil. According to tradition, the white badge (Oribist, with the motto “Defensores de las Leyes”) and the red badge (Riverist) appeared there, the origin of the Blanco and Colorado parties. It was the start of the civil war that led to the Guerra Grande.

hechos/ataque-del-lexington-a-puerto-sol.texto: Attack of the USS Lexington on Puerto Soledad

On 31 December 1831 Captain Silas Duncan of the American corvette USS Lexington landed at Puerto Soledad, in the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), after Luis Vernet had captured, in July, three American fishing vessels (Harriet, Superior and Breakwater) for violating its fishing regulations. The Lexington's log records the destruction of weapons and gunpowder; the colonists later declared greater damage to private property, and Argentine historiography presents it as the looting and destruction of the colony. Buenos Aires, under Rosas's first government, declared the American chargé d'affaires Francis Baylies persona non grata in 1832, and the British occupation of 1833 followed the incident.

lugares/santos-lugares-de-rosas/resumen.texto: Military camp and headquarters that Rosas set up in the town of Santos Lugares de Rosas, today the city of San Martín, northwest of Buenos Aires. It had a troop depot and a prison under Antonino Reyes, and there prisoners were shot by written order of the governor, among them Camila O'Gorman and Ladislao Gutiérrez in 1848.

lugares/caseron-de-rosas/nombre.texto: Caserón de Rosas in Palermo de San Benito

lugares/caseron-de-rosas/resumen.texto: Rosas’s residence on his lands in Palermo de San Benito, built from 1838 at the intersection of today’s Sarmiento and Libertador avenues, from which he governed during the 1840s. After Caseros it housed the Military College and the Naval School. It was demolished on February 3, 1899, the anniversary of Caseros, and its grounds are now part of the Parque Tres de Febrero.

lugares/cerrito-de-la-victoria/resumen.texto: Hill on the outskirts of Montevideo where Manuel Oribe set up his headquarters in 1843 and the Cerrito Government during the Great Siege, with the support of the army of the Argentine Confederation. Today it is a neighborhood of Montevideo.

lugares/iglesia-de-san-ignacio-buenos-ai.texto: Jesuit church in the Manzana de las Luces, the oldest surviving church in the city of Buenos Aires. After the expulsion of 1767 it was put to other uses, and in 1836 Rosas returned it to the Society of Jesus, which occupied it again until its second expulsion in 1843.

lugares/escuela-de-preceptores-de-santia.texto: Normal school founded in Santiago, Chile, in 1842 by the government of Manuel Bulnes, one of the first in the Americas for training teachers. Its first director was the Argentine exile Domingo Faustino Sarmiento.

lugares/universidad-de-chile/resumen.texto: University created by law in 1842 and opened in 1843 in Santiago, with Andrés Bello as its first rector. Several Argentine exiles from the Rosas era, including Sarmiento and Vicente Fidel López, took part in its intellectual life.

lugares/southampton-old-cemetery/resumen.texto: Cemetery in Southampton, England, where Juan Manuel de Rosas was buried in 1877. His remains were exhumed and repatriated to Argentina in 1989.
